extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, constitutional scholars, and educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for assessing constitutional arrangements and the practical effects of checks and balances (comparative discussion of British and American systems). Useful for judging whether a constitution produces decisive, effective, and stable government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singleness and unity of sovereign authority
rubrics_metrics.description: How important singleness and unity are in political action; the excellence of the British Constitution is that it has achieved unity — the sovereign power is single, possible, and good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single, newly-elected House of Commons is described as ultimate authority able to decide on administrative or legislative questions and ensure execution (it appoints and removes the executive). Unity allows easy movement of policy and prevents impediment from interlaced affairs; absence of unity produces motley patchwork and imperfect action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of divided or multiple sovereign authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The splitting of sovereign authority into many parts amounts to there being no sovereign; multiplicity of authorities can prevent ready, deciding power at critical moments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the American constitution: sovereignty retained by states (e.g., control over slavery and suffrage) and divided federal powers produced paralysis during Reconstruction. Multiple repositories of authority (Congress, President, States, Senate for treaties) can create deadlock and inability to remedy urgent problems quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserved state powers and local sovereignty effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers not delegated to the central government are 'reserved to the states respectively' — leading to subordinate governments holding sovereignty over principal matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This decentralization can leave crucial issues (e.g., slavery, suffrage qualification) outside central control, making national remedies difficult and allowing local petty interests and inferior abilities to determine major outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation and subdivision of federal powers (legislative vs administrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: The American constitution separates Congress (law) and the President (administration), with devices like the presidential veto and congressional two-thirds override creating multiple repositories of legislative authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This construction allows variation of supreme legislative authority in different cases and separates administration from legislation, potentially producing inconsistent accountability and variable effectiveness depending on who exerts power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of international and war powers creates distinct sovereignties
rubrics_metrics.description: International policy and treaty-making chiefly belong to the Senate, while Congress declares war but the President as commander-in-chief can continue war and issue paper money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such allocation places greatest international questions in a different part of the state (Senate) and may enable the executive, by precedent and prerogative (e.g., emission of paper money as 'war power'), to continue wars or act without congressional consent, undermining parliamentary control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of constitutional amendment as constraint on remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitution cannot be altered by authorities within it, but only by authorities without it; every alteration must be sanctioned by a complicated proportion of states or legislatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rigidity means obvious evils cannot be quickly remedied; legal fictions and clumsy devices become necessary to evade harmful clauses; practical arguments are hampered by archaic wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety-valve: executive power to alter second chamber composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The head of the executive can overcome the resistance of the second chamber by choosing new members of that chamber — if he does not find a majority, he can make a majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This safety-valve allows the popular will (as represented by the executive) to carry out desires within the constitution that another branch resists; it releases accumulated inhibited power and prevents constitutional suffocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulator: power to dissolve the sovereign chamber
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief executive's power of dissolving the otherwise sovereign chamber enables an appeal from one Parliament to another — 'I will appeal from Parliament No.1 to Parliament No.2.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This regulator impairs the power of an individual Parliament without destroying the species; it checks caprice, party violence, and selfishness by holding members accountable to the electorate and allowing resetting of the representative body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three principal vices of a popular choosing chamber
rubrics_metrics.description: First: caprice in choice and instability of administrations. Second: party organisation required to maintain cohesion, which aggravates sectarianism. Third: peculiar feelings, prejudices, and interests causing parliament to pursue them against national well-being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These vices are the primary faults that constitutional mechanisms (safety-valve, regulator, extrinsic checks) must address; assessing a constitution should consider how it mitigates these three dangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Which authority best checks which vice (intrinsic vs extrinsic checks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Premiers (the executive appointed by Parliament) are best to check caprice because they are most interested in maintaining administration; extrinsic, impartial authorities (e.g., a constitutional king or colonial governor) are better to check party zeal and selfishness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should match the check to the vice: intrinsic appointees resist caprice; detached authorities can restrain sectarianism and self-interest, provided they are morally and intellectually capable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities required in a head exercising dissolving power
rubrics_metrics.description: To dissolve Parliament effectively, the head must be a considerable statesman with natural vigour, incessant industry, and ability to perceive public opinion and complicated policy details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the head lacks statesmanship and industry (as hereditary monarchs often do), the power may be misused or ineffectual; constitutional designers must consider who will possess these qualities before granting such powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perils of hereditary monarchs as extrinsic checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Hereditary kings are often badly educated for business, tempted by pleasure, detached from public affairs, and may carry family taints affecting judgment, making them unreliable judges of public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting decisive checking powers to a hereditary monarch risks blows to delicate cabinet machinery; on great occasions, the premier and Parliament are more likely to be wiser than such a king.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonial governors as a model of extrinsic authority (advantages and costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Colonial governors are often intelligent, impartial, and not tied to local factions, thus able to act as super-parliamentary authorities; but they lack permanent interest in the colony and may govern to protect their own career, leaving colonists feeling misunderstood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An extrinsic authority can check local assemblies effectively, but the advantage is purchased at a heavy price: alienation, lack of local commitment, and governance oriented to the superior power rather than local welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive responsibility ensures execution of parliamentary decrees
rubrics_metrics.description: A parliamentary body that appoints the executive can ensure that its decrees will be executed, because it alone appoints and can remove the executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutions that tie executive appointment/removal to the representative body secure unity between decision and execution, reducing the chance that laws will be ineffectively carried out.
